metadata.dsm5_code: 296.xx (specify current or most recent episode and features)

aeo.what_is: Bipolar I disorder causes episodes of extremely high mood and energy (mania), often with periods of deep depression in between.

content.temporal_criteria: A manic episode lasts at least one week (or any duration if hospitalization is required) with abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and increased energy. Depressive episodes, when present, last at least two weeks. The diagnosis requires only one lifetime manic episode, though most people experience recurrent episodes over time.

confused_with: Major Depressive Disorder — if someone presents first with depression and past manic episodes aren't asked about, they may be misdiagnosed with unipolar depression. The key is screening for any history of decreased sleep with high energy, euphoria, or unusually elevated mood.
ADHD — chronic inattention and hyperactivity from childhood differs from episodic mania with distinct mood elevation, grandiosity, and decreased sleep need that emerges in adolescence or adulthood.

Borderline Personality Disorder — rapid mood shifts in BPD are usually reactive to interpersonal stress and last hours, while bipolar episodes are sustained for days to weeks and often occur without clear triggers.

Substance-induced mania — stimulant use or medication effects can mimic mania, but true bipolar has episodes that occur independently of substances, though substances may worsen or trigger episodes in vulnerable individuals.
Normal high energy or creativity — feeling energized, productive, or passionate about a project is normal; mania involves impairment, dangerously poor judgment, inability to function, or psychosis.
misdiagnosis_explained.clarifying_factors: A detailed longitudinal history capturing distinct episodes (not just traits); collateral information from family or friends who observed past high periods; screening for decreased need for sleep (not just less sleep but feeling energized on 2-3 hours); asking about hospitali zations, spending sprees, risky behavior, or times when others said the person 'wasn't acting like themselves.'
misdiagnosis_explained.timeline_differences: ADHD and personality patterns are lifelong and stable. Bipolar involves clear before-during-after changes: functioning is relatively stable between episodes, deteriorates during mania or depression, then returns to baseline (though residual symptoms are common). Substance effects resolve within days to weeks of stopping use.
misdiagnosis_explained.impairment_differences: Major depression causes withdrawal and trouble functioning because of low mood. Mania can look like things are going well at first (getting lots done, being very social) but can quickly turn into dangerous impulsive acts, overspending, aggression, losing touch with reality, or needing a hospital stay. Mood shifts in borderline personality disorder are distressing but usually don't need a hospital stay unless bipolar disorder is also present.

description.overview: Bipolar I Disorder is characterized by at least one lifetime manic episode, often with recurrent depressive and hypomanic episodes. Mania involves a distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and increased energy/activity, causing marked impairment, need for hospitalization, or psychosis.
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life: A 22-year-old college student stops sleeping, attends every party on campus, signs up for six clubs in one night, and calls her parents at 3 a.m. to announce she's dropping out to start a music career despite never playing an instrument. Her roommates notice she can't finish a sentence without jumping to a new topic.

A 35-year-old accountant who's normally cautious empties his savings to invest in cryptocurrency, books a spontaneous trip to Vegas, sends dozens of flirtatious texts to coworkers, and shows up to work in a neon suit insisting he's about to 'revolutionize finance.' He hasn't slept in four days but feels 'better than ever.'

A 28-year-old mom who's been depressed for months suddenly has boundless energy, repaints the entire house at 2 a.m., enrolls her kids in five new activities, and snaps at her husband for 'not keeping up' with her ideas. She insists she's finally herself again, but her family is alarmed.

A 40-year-old man starts a fight with his boss over a minor comment, quits his job impulsively, spends thousands on a business idea he sketched out in an hour, and drives 100 mph because he 'can't waste time.' His wife finds him on the roof at dawn 'watching the sunrise and thinking about the universe.'

A 19-year-old becomes convinced she has a special connection to God, posts dozens of rambling spiritual messages online, stops eating because she 'doesn't need food anymore,' and tries to give away all her belongings. Her friends call her parents when she talks about 'ascending to a higher plane.'

A 50-year-old teacher who's always been reserved starts every class with a stand-up comedy routine, assigns no homework because 'life is for living,' and proposes marriage to a colleague he barely knows. He's irritable when the principal expresses concern and insists everyone else is 'too uptight.'
common_reactions_to_diagnosis: Shock or disbelief, especially if they've only experienced depression and didn't realize past 'great' periods were mania.
Relief that their extreme behaviors have an explanation and aren't just character flaws.
Grief about needing lifelong treatment and the reality of a chronic condition.
Fear of future episodes and losing control again.
Resistance to the diagnosis, especially if manic episodes felt good or productive.
Shame about things said or done during mania that damaged relationships or finances.
Anger or frustration about being misdiagnosed with depression for years.

content.diagnostic_criteria: A. At least 1 manic episode (lasting at least 1 week, or any length of time if a hospital stay is needed) with unusually high, expansive or irritable mood and more energy, plus at least 3 (at least 4 if the mood is only irritable) of: feeling overly important or powerful; needing much less sleep; fast, pressured talking; racing thoughts that jump between ideas; being easily distracted; a big increase in activity toward goals, or restlessness; risky activities. B. The episode causes serious problems, needs a hospital stay, or includes losing touch with reality. C. It is not caused by a substance or medical condition. Episodes of major depression are common but are not needed for the diagnosis.
content.prevalence: About 1 in 100 people have bipolar I disorder at some point in life, and it is about as common in men as in women. It is often missed or mistaken for something else early on.
content.age_of_onset: It usually starts in the late teens or early adulthood, but it can start at any age.
content.prognosis: Recurrent, episodic course with variable inter-episode recovery. Early recognition, maintenance mood stabilization, psychotherapy, and substance-use management improve functional outcomes and reduce relapse/suicide risk.

circuitry: Dysregulation in fronto-limbic networks (ventromedial/dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, amygdala, anterior cingulate) affecting emotion regulation and impulse control.
Abnormal reward and salience processing in striatum and insula; altered thalamo-cortical synchronization.
neurochemistry: Perturbations in monoamines (dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine) and glutamate/GABA balance.
Neuroendocrine and inflammatory signaling differences (HPA axis, cytokines) associated with mood state changes.
neurobiology.genetic_environmental: High heritability (polygenic). Sleep/circadian disruption, substance use, and psychosocial stress act as triggers in vulnerable individuals.

history_psychosocial: Longitudinal timeline of mood episodes, sleep/circadian patterns, psychosis, hospitalizations, suicidality, and functional impairment.
Family psychiatric history; trauma and psychosocial stressors; substance use (alcohol, cannabis, stimulants).
medical_assessment: Rule out secondary causes and substances: medication review (steroids, stimulants), urine toxicology as indicated.
Screen labs: CBC, CMP, TSH, pregnancy test when relevant; consider B12, folate; ECG if cardiac risk/antipsychotic use.
standardized_measures: Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS) for mania; Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) or PHQ-9 for depression.
Mood Disorder Questionnaire (MDQ) for lifetime bipolar features; Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) for suicide risk.
risk_stratification: Hospitalize for severe mania, psychosis, suicidal/homicidal risk, severe agitation, or marked impairment/refusal of care.
differential_diagnosis: Substance/medication-induced mood disorder; ADHD; Borderline Personality Disorder; Schizoaffective Disorder; Bipolar II; Cyclothymic Disorder; medical causes (hyperthyroidism, Cushing’s, neurologic disease).
evaluation.team_and_process: Shared management among psychiatry, primary care, and (when relevant) OB-GYN/neurology; include family/partners for collateral and relapse planning.

mania_hypomania: Decreased need for sleep with high energy
Pressured speech and flight of ideas
depression: Low mood or losing interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy
Changes in sleep or appetite; restlessness or moving and thinking slowly
psychosis_possible: Mood-congruent or incongruent delusions/hallucinations during manic or depressive episodes

severity_levels.mild: Symptoms noticeable but manageable; limited functional impact; outpatient care.
severity_levels.moderate: Clear functional impairment in work/school/relationships; may require intensive outpatient or partial hospital.
severity_levels.severe: Marked impairment, psychosis, or dangerousness; often requires inpatient stabilization.

environmental: Sleep deprivation, shift work, jet lag

impact_on_life.school_work: Absenteeism, erratic performance, financial/legal problems from risky behavior.
impact_on_life.social: Relationship conflict, stigma, impulsive decisions with lasting consequences.
impact_on_life.medical: Metabolic/cardiovascular risk from medications and lifestyle; injuries during mania.

acute_mania: A mood stabilizer or an atypical antipsychotic is usually tried first; a combination may be used for severe mania or mania with loss of touch with reality.
Examples: lithium; valproate; antipsychotics such as haloperidol, risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole, ziprasidone, cariprazine, asenapine.
bipolar_depression: Quetiapine; lurasidone (often with mood stabilizer); cariprazine; lamotrigine (more for prevention, modest acute effect).
Antidepressants on their own are usually avoided; if one is used, it is combined with a mood stabilizer and watched closely for a switch into mania.
maintenance_relapse_prevention: Lithium (suicide risk reduction); valproate; lamotrigine; quetiapine; aripiprazole and other SGAs as indicated.
Learning about the condition, tracking your personal early warning signs, and support with taking treatment as planned.
psychotherapy: CBT tailored for bipolar depression and adherence.
Interpersonal and Social Rhythm Therapy (IPSRT) for circadian stabilization.
Family-Focused Therapy (FFT) to reduce expressed emotion and improve communication.
Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) skills for emotion regulation and impulsivity.
neuromodulation: Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT) for severe, psychotic, or treatment-resistant mania or depression, or when rapid response is needed.
Repetitive TMS as an add-on for bipolar depression (guided by a specialist; research is still developing).
lifestyle_interventions: Strict sleep–wake routines; light hygiene; limit substances and caffeine.
Regular aerobic activity; nutrition; weight/metabolic monitoring.
Structured daily routines; stress management; digital relapse tracking.
medications: Mood stabilizers: lithium, valproate/divalproex, lamotrigine, carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine (selected cases).
Atypical antipsychotics: quetiapine, lurasidone, olanzapine, risperidone, paliperidone, aripiprazole, ziprasidone, asenapine, cariprazine; clozapine for refractory cases with careful monitoring.
Monitoring: lithium levels/renal/thyroid; valproate levels/LFTs/platelets; carbamazepine CBC/LFTs/sodium; SGA metabolic labs (weight, lipids, glucose).
Pregnancy planning: valproate is avoided in pregnancy when possible; talk about birth control and medicines that can harm a developing baby; plan care around pregnancy and birth.
care_coordination: Safety planning and suicide risk management.
Shared decision-making; advance directives for relapse plans.
Communication with family/supports (with consent) and employers/schools for accommodations as needed.

treatment_goals: Rapidly stabilize acute mania or bipolar depression.
Prevent relapse and reduce episode frequency/severity.
Keep side effects and other health problems as low as possible.
Restore role functioning and quality of life; reduce suicide risk.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Presenting only with depression; hypomanic/manic history not elicited.
Attributing decreased sleep and energy to work stress or ADHD without assessing euphoria/irritability and impairment.
Substance use obscuring manic symptoms; episodes mistaken for personality or situational crises.
Cultural norms of high energy/expressiveness masking pathologic elevation.
overdiagnosis_factors: Diagnosing based on brief irritability or stimulant intoxication without sustained manic syndrome.
Labeling ADHD, Borderline Personality Disorder, or cyclothymia as Bipolar I without clear manic episodes.
Using screening tools (e.g., MDQ) as sole basis without clinical interview.
Misattributing antidepressant side effects or sleep loss to mania without full criteria.

episode_specifiers: With mixed features (signs of mania and depression at the same time)
With psychotic features (losing touch with reality), either matching the mood or not
With peripartum onset (starting during pregnancy or soon after birth)

warning_signs: Reduced need for sleep without fatigue; escalating goal-directed activity.
Increased spending, risky sex, or impulsive decisions.
Starting to lose touch with reality, or agitation; thoughts of suicide during depression or mixed episodes.
self_help_strategies: Consistent sleep–wake times and daily routines; avoid night shifts.
Track early warning signs (sleep change, irritability, spending); share plan with supports.
Limit alcohol/cannabis/stimulants; build a crisis plan and support network.

adolescence: Often first manic episode; higher risk of substance use and school disruption; strong family involvement and school accommodations help.
young_adulthood: Role transitions (college/work/relationships); adherence and sleep regularity are central to relapse prevention.
midlife_older_adults: Other health conditions and taking many medicines need extra care; checks of memory and thinking, kidneys and thyroid (with lithium), and weight, blood sugar and cholesterol with newer antipsychotics.

first_person_statements: I felt invincible and like I'd unlocked the secrets of the universe, but I was actually making terrible decisions that nearly destroyed my life.
I couldn't understand why everyone was so worried—I felt better than I'd ever felt—but looking back, I was completely out of control.
The depression after mania was the worst part: not only did I feel suicidal, but I had to deal with the wreckage I'd caused while manic.
I went from being unable to get out of bed to being unable to sit still for even a minute. The swings were exhausting and terrifying.
People kept telling me to slow down and sleep, but I genuinely didn't feel tired. My brain was on fire with ideas I had to act on immediately.
I ruined my credit, lost friends, and quit my job during one manic episode. Recovery has been about rebuilding everything, not just my mood.

comparisons: Imagine your brain's gas pedal getting stuck to the floor during mania—you're speeding uncontrollably in every direction—and then during depression, the engine dies completely and you can't move at all.

It's like a psychological roller coaster you can't get off: the manic highs feel exhilarating until you realize you're in danger, and the depressive crashes leave you broken and unable to see a way forward.
Think of it as your mood regulation system swinging between extremes like a pendulum that's lost its center, and no amount of willpower can stop the swing once it's started.

It's like living in two completely different realities—one where everything is possible and you're unstoppable, and another where everything is hopeless and you can barely function—and neither one reflects who you actually are.

faqs.question: Bipolar I vs. Bipolar II: what's the difference?
faqs.answer: Bipolar I involves at least one full manic episode (severe, often requiring hospitalization, possibly with psychosis). Bipolar II involves hypomania (milder elevated mood lasting at least four days) plus major depression. Both are serious, but Bipolar I mania is more severe and impairing.

faqs.question: Can you have Bipolar I with only manic episodes and no depression?
faqs.answer: Yes, though it's less common. The diagnosis requires only one manic episode. However, most people with Bipolar I will experience depressive episodes at some point, and many people spend more time depressed than manic over their lifetime.

faqs.question: Bipolar I vs. ADHD: how do you tell them apart?
faqs.answer: ADHD symptoms (inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity) are lifelong and relatively consistent. Bipolar I involves distinct episodes with a clear before, during, and after: during mania there's elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, and often reckless behavior that's very different from the person's baseline. ADHD doesn't include mood episodes.

faqs.question: Bipolar I vs. Borderline Personality Disorder: what's the difference?
faqs.answer: BPD involves rapid mood shifts (minutes to hours) usually triggered by interpersonal stress, with persistent identity issues and fear of abandonment. Bipolar I mood episodes last days to weeks, often occur without clear triggers, and involve sustained changes in energy, sleep, and goal-directed activity rather than just emotional reactivity.

faqs.question: Can Bipolar I be cured?
faqs.answer: There's no cure, but with proper treatment—mood stabilizers, therapy, and lifestyle management—many people achieve long periods of stability and lead fulfilling lives. The goal is managing episodes, reducing their frequency and severity, and maintaining functioning between episodes.

faqs.question: What triggers a manic episode?
faqs.answer: Common triggers include sleep disruption, stopping medication, high stress, substance use (especially stimulants), antidepressants without a mood stabilizer, seasonal changes, and major life events. For some people, episodes can occur without any obvious trigger.

faqs.question: How long does a manic episode last?
faqs.answer: Without treatment, mania can last weeks to months. With treatment, symptoms often begin to improve within days to a couple of weeks, though full stabilization may take longer. Hospitalization is sometimes needed to ensure safety during severe episodes.

faqs.question: Do I have to take medication forever?
faqs.answer: Most people with Bipolar I need long-term mood stabilizers to prevent relapse. Stopping medication is a leading cause of recurrence. Some people may attempt cautious tapers after years of stability, but this requires close monitoring. The decision should be made collaboratively with your treatment team.

faqs.question: Can therapy alone treat Bipolar I?
faqs.answer: Therapy is essential for learning to manage the condition, recognize early warning signs, and address psychosocial stressors, but it's typically not sufficient alone for Bipolar I. Medication is usually necessary to prevent or shorten mood episodes and reduce the risk of relapse.

faqs.question: Is Bipolar I genetic?
faqs.answer: Yes, there's a strong genetic component. Having a first-degree relative with bipolar disorder significantly increases risk. However, it's not a single gene—many genetic variants plus environmental factors (stress, trauma, substance use) interact to influence whether someone develops the condition.

faqs.question: Can you work or go to school with Bipolar I?
faqs.answer: Yes, many people with Bipolar I work and attend school successfully, especially with stable treatment and accommodations (flexible schedules, reduced course load during rough patches). Severe or frequent episodes can make it harder, but recovery and functioning are absolutely possible.

faqs.question: What does it mean to have mania and depression at the same time?
faqs.answer: This is called having mixed features (mania and depression together): symptoms of both at the same time or switching quickly within the same episode. For example, high energy and racing thoughts alongside hopelessness and thoughts of suicide. These episodes are especially dangerous and harder to treat.

faqs.question: What's rapid cycling in Bipolar I?
faqs.answer: Rapid cycling means having four or more mood episodes (manic, hypomanic, or depressive) within a year. It's harder to treat and often linked to factors like untreated hypothyroidism, antidepressant use without mood stabilizers, or substance use.

faqs.question: Can antidepressants make Bipolar I worse?
faqs.answer: Yes. Antidepressants alone (without a mood stabilizer) can trigger mania, hypomania, or rapid cycling in people with Bipolar I. If depression is severe, antidepressants may be used cautiously alongside a mood stabilizer, but the risk–benefit balance must be carefully managed.

faqs.question: What should I do if I think I'm becoming manic?
faqs.answer: Contact your psychiatrist or treatment team immediately. Early intervention—adjusting medication, increasing sleep, reducing stimulation—can sometimes prevent a full manic episode. If you're having dangerous thoughts or behaviors, go to an emergency room or call 988.

faqs.question: Can substance use cause Bipolar I?
faqs.answer: Substance use doesn't cause Bipolar I, but stimulants, alcohol, and cannabis can trigger episodes in vulnerable individuals or mimic bipolar symptoms. Many people with Bipolar I struggle with substance use, which complicates diagnosis and treatment and worsens outcomes.

faqs.question: Is Bipolar I a disability?
faqs.answer: Bipolar I can qualify as a disability under the ADA if it substantially limits major life activities. This can provide access to workplace or academic accommodations and, in some cases, disability benefits. Severity and functional impact vary widely among individuals.

faqs.question: Can you have psychosis in Bipolar I?
faqs.answer: Yes. Severe manic or depressive episodes can include losing touch with reality, such as delusions (false beliefs) or hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that aren't there). These usually match the mood (for example, believing you have special powers during mania) and fade when the mood episode is treated.

faqs.question: What's the suicide risk in Bipolar I?
faqs.answer: Bipolar I has one of the highest suicide risks of any psychiatric condition, particularly during depressive and mixed episodes. Lithium has been shown to reduce suicide risk. Safety planning, close monitoring, and prompt treatment of depression are critical.

faqs.question: Can Bipolar I get better with age?
faqs.answer: Episode frequency and severity can sometimes decrease with age, especially with consistent treatment. However, untreated or poorly managed bipolar often worsens over time, with more frequent episodes and longer recovery periods. Early, sustained treatment improves long-term outcomes.

real_life_examples.person: A 20-year-old college junior stopped sleeping for three consecutive nights during finals week. She felt euphoric and invincible, convinced she'd ace every exam without studying. She spent $3,000 online buying gifts for acquaintances, signed up to run for student government, and sent long, rambling emails to professors about 'revolutionary ideas.' Her roommate found her dancing alone at 4 a.m. and called her parents. She was hospitalized, started on lithium and olanzapine, and after stabilization began IPSRT to manage sleep and routines. She returned to school the following semester with accommodations and has been stable for two years.

A 34-year-old graphic designer had been treated for depression for years with an SSRI. During a routine visit, his psychiatrist asked if he'd ever had periods of high energy. He recalled a week after a big promotion when he barely slept, felt 'on top of the world,' drove recklessly, and almost got into a fight with a stranger. His SSRI was stopped, and he was started on quetiapine and lamotrigine. CBT and family-focused therapy helped him and his wife recognize early warning signs. He's had no manic episodes in three years.

A 27-year-old teacher with no past mental health problems suddenly quit her job, maxed out her credit cards on a trip to Europe, and believed she was destined to become a famous singer despite never performing. She became irritable and suspicious when her family questioned her. She was hospitalized against her will after threatening a stranger. Risperidone and lithium were started, and learning about the condition helped her understand the episode. She slowly rebuilt her finances, found a new teaching job, and now takes her medicine consistently and tracks her sleep carefully.

A 45-year-old accountant with a history of severe depressions and one prior hospitalization for mania was stable on lithium for five years. After a stressful project, he decided he 'felt fine' and stopped his medication. Within two weeks, he was sleeping two hours a night, taking on freelance work he couldn't finish, and fighting with his wife. His psychiatrist restarted lithium and added aripiprazole. Couples therapy helped repair the relationship, and he now uses a pill organizer and attends monthly medication management to prevent future lapses.

A 19-year-old was brought to the ER by campus police after she climbed onto the roof of her dorm, saying she could fly. She had stopped eating, believing she no longer needed food, and had been posting end-of-the-world religious messages online. She was diagnosed with bipolar I disorder with loss of touch with reality, treated with haloperidol and valproate, and after discharge took part in DBT to manage impulsive behavior. She took a medical leave, became stable, and returned to college part-time. She's now applying to graduate school and speaks up for mental health awareness on campus.

content.when_to_seek_help: Get checked soon if you have a new, severe loss of sleep without feeling tired, spending or risk-taking that keeps growing, or a period of depression. Get urgent help for mania with unsafe behavior, losing touch with reality, or thoughts of harming yourself or someone else.

positive_factors: Early sustained mood stabilization (e.g., lithium) and psychotherapy
Supportive family/low expressed emotion; regular routines
challenging_factors: Substance use at the same time, mania and depression symptoms together, or fast cycling between episodes
High psychosocial stress or hostile/critical family climate
